question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: In the case of a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure, the cranial nerves most likely affected are III, IV, V1, and VI. This can lead to ophthalmoplegia, which includes impaired eye movements and potentially an absent corneal reflex due to involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Therefore, the most likely physical examination finding would be an absent left corneal reflex. Numbness of the left cheek is less likely as it involves the maxillary branch (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, which is not typically affected by superior orbital fissure compression. Preserved left lateral gaze is unlikely due to potential impairment of the abducens nerve (VI), which controls lateral eye movement. Complete loss of vision in the left eye is not expected as the optic nerve (II) is not typically involved in superior orbital fissure syndrome. Decreased sense of smell is unrelated as it involves the olfactory nerve (I), which is not affected in this scenario. Therefore, the most consensus-aligned finding is an absent left corneal reflex.
analysis: In this scenario, the patient has a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. The superior orbital fissure is a key anatomical structure through which cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve), and VI (abducens) pass. Compression in this area can lead to superior orbital fissure syndrome, characterized by ophthalmoplegia (paralysis or weakness of the eye muscles), ptosis, and sensory loss in the distribution of V1. The absent left corneal reflex is a result of the involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for the sensory component of the corneal reflex. Other options, such as numbness of the left cheek (V2 involvement), preserved left lateral gaze (VI involvement), and complete loss of vision (optic nerve involvement), are less likely given the specific location of the fracture and the nerves typically affected. Decreased sense of smell is unrelated as it involves the olfactory nerve (I), which is not affected in this scenario. Therefore, the most likely physical examination finding is an absent left corneal reflex.
